I've heard Tate's thesis mentioned as a possible student project for formalization, and its eventual inclusion into Mathlib would be an elegant way to get the functional equation of the Dedekind zeta function. I don't know if people are pushing on the analytic method of proving the functional equation, just what I can see in mathlib which seems like there is a long ways to go. Although Tate's thesis is separate from FLT and was known a very long time before the 1980s, it would out of necessity require leveraging some of the major theorems from FLT which are not in Mathlib.

Would it make sense to set this up as a mini-project adjacent to FLT? There would have to be at least some connection between the two projects because otherwise the Tate ends up being too large of a project and repeats too much difficult work.

I could see a couple of advantages to setting up a mini project: it would familiarize students and new-to-lean users with the api for FLT, and it would ensure that code written by a team of beginners is written to a standard which would allow it to someday merge with Mathlib. Because of the amount of overlap with FLT work it might be a gentle on ramp for people who want to contribute to FLT.

The catch would be a couple more senior reviewers would need to approve pull requests to that side project repo, which is a (mostly) thankless time sink for people who already have a huge job. Without experienced people having some level of involvement a beginner project is likely to turn into an unsalvageable mess.
cc @Riccardo Brasca @Filippo A. E. Nuccio, who I think have plans to supervise this as a project, iirc.

I don't need it for FLT so would be reluctant to host it (and hence have to maintain it) as part of FLT. We do however have a bunch of adele-related content in FLT which would be useful for Tate's thesis, although this content will ultimately be upstreamed to mathlib.

Johan Commelin said:

cc Riccardo Brasca Filippo A. E. Nuccio, who I think have plans to supervise this as a project, iirc.

Yes, indeed: a PhD student co-supervised by @Riccardo Brasca and myself will start working on Tate's thesis in September with the goal of making it into Mathlib. I think it would be unfortunate for them if there are several parallel projects formalising the same material.
There has been some discussion recently of people being able to "claim" projects -- maybe this project should be "claimed" somehow?
Yes, I think this is a very good idea! But to the best of my understanding nothing of the sort exists yet officially. We'll do as soon as possible.

A quick remark/update relating both to FLT and Tate's thesis:

Brauer-Nesbitt guarantees that two Galois representations have isomorphic semisimplifications if their characteristic polynomials agree for all elements (or, when char=0 or >n, if their traces agree). With Chebotarev, this reduces to just needing the traces of Frobenius to agree. However, to prove Chebotarev, one needs non-vanishing at 1 of one-dimensional Artin L-function associated with the character $\chi$ of Gal(K(\zeta_n)/K), which in turn requires analytic continuation of the L-function beyond Re(s)>1.

The update is that I have completed a formalization (without any sorries) of all these ingredients, which includes: Brauer-Nesbitt, Newton's identities relating traces to characteristic polynomials, and most importantly, the Chebotarev density theorem (without using class field theory, following the Lenstra-Stevenhagen article, and thus extremely ad hoc., but works!). The proof uses the cyclotomic case as a base, and juggles between Artin L-functions and Hecke L-functions associated with cyclotomic extensions without actually needing Artin reciprocity. The code currently spans over 11k lines. I am in the process of refactoring it to make it faster and more concise, and hopefully this will be completed within 3 weeks.

Back to Tate's thesis: If one had Tate's thesis (or even Hecke's original 1920 argument) available, much pain would have been saved. I had to use the geometry of numbers to prove that cyclotomic Artin L-functions has analytic continuation to Re(s)>1-1/[K:\mathbb{Q}], which, although sufficient for the proof of Chebotarev, is tedious and hard to generalize, spanning about 5k lines. Really looking forward to seeing the Tate's thesis in Lean!
That’s very impressive! I didn’t realize we even had Artin L functions formalized yet.
For which density do you have Chebotarev? With @Chris Birkbeck and @Xavier Roblot we also have it (around 10K lines of code) and also in the process of cleaning it.
@Ryan Smith Yes Artin L-functions I also formalized... but for this project only the one-dim case is needed. I did formalize the general definition and restrict to the one-dim case though.
@Riccardo Brasca Dirichlet density. I didn't know you were doing this! Sorry about that.
Well it's already done, since a couple of weeks
You can see the discussion here: #PrimeNumberTheorem+ > What route to take to Chebotarev?

anyway we are in the process of slowly PRing stuff to mathlib, after cleaning it
